paras: The attempted lynching of Albert Thomas and George Campbell took place at Fairmont, West Virginia, on the night of August 11-12, 1900, when a crowd of several hundred went to the Marion County jail to hang the two young Black men, who were accused of shooting two Baltimore & Ohio railroad men that afternoon. Officers had already removed the prisoners, and the crowd searched the jail and dispersed. The two were moved to the Ohio County jail at Wheeling, where they were still held awaiting trial in mid-September.

According to Fairmont dispatches, the two men had tried to board an eastbound freight at Farmington the evening before, in company with three white men, and fired at the brakeman who put them off. Detective Charles Lilley of Grafton traced them to Fairmont and, with Henry Downey, a company employee there, tried to arrest them about 4 p.m. on Saturday, August 11.

In the railroad men's version, the two broke free and opened fire with .32 and .38 revolvers, wounding Downey in the breast and arm and Lilley in the side and arm. General Yardmaster Riggs led a pursuit by engine, and a party including Chief Fleming and Constable Jones found the men hiding in bushes above town. The Times reported that when brought in they "were surrounded by an angry mob" while crowds awaited Downey's death.

That night, the Morgantown New Dominion wrote, a report spread that Downey had died, and "a mob of five hundred men at once started for the jail to hang the murderers." The Wheeling Register put the crowd at four hundred and the time at about 2 a.m. Sunday. Anticipating the move, county officers had taken the prisoners out; Campbell later said they were removed "when the mob was forming" and hidden for about three hours in a country house. The crowd searched the jail, raised "considerable disturbance," and dispersed.

The men were returned to Fairmont at daylight and that afternoon were taken by deputies over the B&O to the Ohio County jail at Wheeling. The Register traced the route through Gray's Flats and Barracksville, where tickets were bought for Moundsville, the destination some papers reported.

Interviewed in their cells, Thomas, who gave his age as seventeen and his home as Philadelphia, said he fired a .38 "to scare" the two men because he thought he was being arrested for vagrancy. Campbell, twenty-two and from Larimore, North Dakota, told the Intelligencer it was "self defense" but told the Register that they had not shot at anyone. Lilley, for his part, said he had fired three or four shots at "the big negro" and missed.

Excitement at Fairmont subsided within days as Downey began to recover, though the New Dominion reported that Mrs. Downey was disappointed that the crowd had failed to secure the men. Judge Mason planned to consult the Marion County bar about a special grand jury but said the case would not be tried until public feeling subsided. The men stayed in Wheeling because lynching was still feared, and by September 13 Downey was reported out of danger while the accused awaited trial at Fairmont. No report of an indictment, a trial or arrests in the crowd appears in the coverage.

The story ran almost entirely in West Virginia papers, with Fairmont specials also reaching two Washington papers. The first reports treated a lynching as the expected result if Downey died, under headlines such as "A LYNCHING PROBABLE" and "Lynching Not Improbable if the Wounded Man Should Die." They called the two men "colored tramps" and "would-be murderers," and the Wheeling Sunday Register said they had confessed.

The Morgantown New Dominion wrote that the mob would have hanged the "guilty men" "without delay," later called them "negro outlaws" and "habitual criminals," and said that if Downey died "justice will be promptly meted out to them." The Wheeling papers, by contrast, headlined the threat itself, "THREATENED WITH LYNCHING," and printed the prisoners' own statements.

Accounts differ on the men's names, printed as Albert Thorne or Thorn and Charles or James Campbell, and on their homes, but the Wheeling papers that interviewed them give Albert Thomas of Philadelphia and George Campbell.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Albert Thomas and George Campbell
bases: A crowd of 400 to 500 went to the Marion County jail at Fairmont to hang two jailed Black men accused of shooting two railroad men, searched the building, and dispersed when it found that officers had removed them (A3, A5, A7).

No one was killed: the officers removed the two prisoners before the crowd of 400-500 reached and searched the jail, and both were later reported held in Wheeling awaiting trial (A5, A7, A17); this was an attempted lynching acting on the shooting accusation (A3).

Separate specials to the Intelligencer, the Register, the New Dominion and the Clarksburg Telegram agree that a crowd searched the Fairmont jail to lynch the men and that officers had removed them (A3, A5, A7, A12); the shooting itself is reported by independent Fairmont specials (A1, A2, A8).

accounts.label: Fairmont specials and wire
accounts.gist: Two Black tramps who had fired on trainmen at Farmington fired on Lilley and Downey when the two tried to arrest them, fled, and were run down by railroad men and officers; they 'confess' to the shooting.

accounts.label: Albert Thomas
accounts.gist: He drew his .38 and fired 'to scare' a detective and another man coming toward him, thinking it was a vagrancy arrest.

accounts.label: George Campbell
accounts.gist: It was 'self defense'; in another interview he said he and Thomas did not shoot at anyone. He described being taken from the jail as the mob formed and hidden in a country house.

accounts.label: Detective Lilley
accounts.gist: When they overtook the two men he fired three or four shots at 'the big negro' and missed; a bullet was stopped by a memorandum book over his heart.

framing.detail: Headlines such as 'A LYNCHING PROBABLE' and 'Lynching Not Improbable if the Wounded Man Should Die' forecast a lynching as a matter of course, and the New Dominion said the men 'would have been hung without delay', while the Wheeling papers reported the removal as a precaution and printed the prisoners' own statements.
Morgantown's New Dominion called the men 'negro outlaws' and 'habitual criminals' and said that if Downey died 'justice will be promptly meted out to them'.
